question: Ktorý nápoj si ľudia v lietadle objednávajú takmer tak často ako pivo, hoci doma by si ho väčšina z nich nikdy nedala?
source_excerpt: Lufthansa served about 53,000 gallons of tomato juice a year, just shy of the 59,000 gallons of beer they serve each year.

extra.why_interesting: Players have seen fellow passengers order tomato juice on a plane, or done it themselves, without ever wondering why. The surprise is that it nearly matches beer, and that the reason is physical: the cabin changes how your tongue works.
extra.verification_notes: Lufthansa data (about 53,000 gal tomato juice vs 59,000 gal beer yearly) supports tomato juice as nearly as popular as beer in flight, and it is disliked at ground level; see https://www.nbcphiladelphia.com/news/local/whyy-why-do-we-drink-tomato-juice-on-planes/67404/

explanation: V suchom vzduchu a pri nižšom tlaku v kabíne slabne vnímanie slaného a sladkého, takže paradajková šťava zrazu chutí plnšie a lepšie. Lufthansa jej ročne naleje okolo 1,8 milióna litrov.

question: Bratislavské letisko nesie meno muža, ktorý pozoroval hviezdy aj z vrcholu Mont Blancu a neskôr zahynul pri havárii lietadla. Kto to bol?
source_excerpt: Bratislavské letisko nesie meno M. R. Štefánika od 21. júla 1993

extra.why_interesting: Every Slovak knows Štefánik as a general and pilot, but few picture him hauling telescopes up Mont Blanc. The astronomer clue misleads at first, then the plane crash and the airport snap it into place, giving an 'I can work this out' moment.
extra.verification_notes: Bratislava airport has been named after M. R. Štefánik since 1993; he was an astronomer who worked on Mont Blanc and died in a 1919 plane crash (https://www.teraz.sk/ekonomika/pred-30-rokmi-pomenovali-bratislavske-l/729371-clanok.html).

explanation: Štefánik bol najprv uznávaný astronóm, ktorý kvôli pozorovaniam vystupoval na Mont Blanc a cestoval až na Tahiti. Generálom a letcom sa stal až potom. Zahynul v roku 1919 pri Ivanke pri Dunaji, len kúsok od miesta, kde dnes stojí letisko s jeho menom.
